introduction: Xenophon, Oeconomicus 8.11–20 and 9.2–10. Read this controlled course adaptation with the glosses, then revisit its source and historical setting on page three.

Ischomachus’ ship comparison and household organization are adapted from his report to Socrates. The concise questions about objects are course wording. His wife’s views reach us through a male speaker and author, not an independent transcript.
δύναμαι, κεῖμαι, and ἐπίσταμαι connect ability and knowledge with the practical arrangement of objects.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ἰσχόμαχος τῷ Σωκράτει περὶ τῆς οἰκίας λέγει. «ποῦ κεῖται τὰ σκεύη;» οὐ μικρὰ αὕτη ἡ ἐρώτησίς ἐστιν. ὁ γὰρ ζητῶν πολλάκις οὐ δύναται εὑρίσκειν.

gloss.english: lie, are situated; neuter plural subject

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ἰσχόμαχος ναῦν Φοινικικὴν εἶδεν. ἐν τῇ νηὶ πολλὰ σκεύη ἔκειτο· ἕκαστον δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ χώραν εἶχεν. ὁ τῶν σκευῶν φύλαξ ἠπίστατο τὰς χώρας.
Ἡ ναῦς ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ κινεῖται. ὅμως δὲ οἱ ναῦται τὰ χρήσιμα λαβεῖν δύνανται. ἡ δὲ οἰκία μένει· τί οὖν κωλύει καὶ ἐνθάδε τάξιν εἶναι;
Ἡ γυνὴ τὴν τάξιν ζητεῖ. ὁ Ἰσχόμαχος τὰ οἰκήματα αὐτῇ δεικνύει. ὁ μὲν σῖτος ἐν ξηρῷ κεῖται, ὁ δὲ οἶνος ἐν ψυχρῷ. τὰ δὲ ἱμάτια ἄλλην χώραν ἔχει.
Οἱ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ οὐ πάντες τὰ αὐτὰ ἐπίστανται. ἡ μὲν γυνὴ τὰ ἔργα σκοπεῖ, οἱ δὲ δοῦλοι πονοῦσιν. ἡ τάξις καὶ μνήμης καὶ ἐργασίας δεῖται.
Νῦν ἡμεῖς τὴν τάξιν ἐξετάζομεν. τίς εὑρίσκει τὰ σκεύη; τίς αὐτὰ κομίζει; τίς κελεύει; τὸ «δύναμαι» καὶ τὸ «ἐπίσταμαι» οὐ τὸ αὐτὸ δηλοῖ.

reading.translation:
Ischomachus speaks with Socrates about the household. “Where are the objects?” This is not a small question. For someone searching often cannot find them.

Ischomachus saw a Phoenician ship. Much equipment lay in the ship, and each item had its own place. The keeper of the equipment knew the places.

The ship moves on the sea. Nevertheless the sailors can get useful things. But the house stays still; what then prevents order here too?

His wife asks for the arrangement. Ischomachus shows her the rooms. Grain lies in a dry place, wine in a cool place. Clothing has another place.

Not everyone in the house knows the same things. The wife oversees the work, while enslaved workers labor. Order requires both memory and work.

Now we examine the arrangement. Who finds the objects? Who carries them? Who gives orders? “I am able” and “I know how” do not mean the same thing.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — τάξις: an arrangement people can use

blocks.title: τάξις: an arrangement people can use
body: τάξις can mean arrangement, order, or a position in a formation. Its family includes τάττω, “arrange.” In household discussion, order concerns relationships among things and people, not merely visual tidiness.
A useful arrangement is intelligible to the people using it. Contrast the label for order with the verbs that describe the work required to maintain it.

sections.title: 1. δύναμαι: capacity and its limits
body: δύναμαι means “be able” and uses middle forms. It commonly takes an infinitive: δύναται εὑρίσκειν, “she can find.” The infinitive does not acquire the person and number of the finite verb.
Learn the present δύναμαι, δύνασαι, δύναται, δυνάμεθα, δύνασθε, δύνανται. Learn the imperfect forms: ἐδυνάμην, ἐδύνασο, ἐδύνατο; ἠδυνάμην and related variants also occur in Attic.

sections.title: 2. κεῖμαι: where things lie
body: κεῖμαι means “lie, be situated,” often describing the resulting location of something placed. It is not the ordinary active verb “put.” Use τίθημι when someone places an object; use κεῖμαι when describing where it lies.

The forms κεῖται and κεῖνται are especially useful in a household inventory. The imperfect ἔκειτο describes where something was lying or situated. Follow the location with a suitable phrase such as ἐν plus dative.

sections.title: 3. ἐπίσταμαι: knowing how
body: ἐπίσταμαι means “know, understand,” including knowing how to perform a task. With an infinitive it expresses practical knowledge: ἐπίσταται κομίζειν, “she knows how to carry.” This is different from δύναται, which emphasizes capacity or opportunity.
The present is ἐπίσταμαι, ἐπίστασαι, ἐπίσταται, ἐπιστάμεθα, ἐπίστασθε, ἐπίστανται. The imperfect is ἠπιστάμην, ἠπίστασο, ἠπίστατο, ἠπιστάμεθα, ἠπίστασθε, ἠπίσταντο.

sections.title: 4. Matching verb and complement
body: An infinitive can complete an idea left unfinished by a verb: “can ...,” “knows how ...,” “wishes ...”. In ordinary same-subject examples, the subject of the infinitive is the subject of the finite verb.

Contrast ability, skill, and location. δύναται κομίζειν says that carrying is possible; ἐπίσταται κομίζειν says the person knows how; κεῖται identifies where an object lies. Translate the full relationship, not just an isolated dictionary entry.

sections.title: Meet the Oeconomicus: Ischomachus’s account
body: Later in the Oeconomicus, Socrates recounts his conversation with Ischomachus about household management. In chapters 8–9, arrangement and finding things become vivid examples of order. We hear a man describe the household’s practices and his wife’s role through a reported conversation.

The dialogue’s twenty-one chapters move from the meaning of wealth to the organization of an estate. Socrates first questions Critobulus about whether possessions actually benefit their owner. He then recounts an extended conversation with Ischomachus, a prosperous gentleman-farmer, about marriage, household organization, agriculture, and directing other people’s work. The shift lets a philosophical question become a tour of everyday decisions.

Read with two questions in mind: what makes management effective, and whose interests define success? Ischomachus describes his young wife’s education and the work of enslaved people from the position of a male household head. His account gives access to ideals of cooperation and order while also revealing unequal authority. Socrates’ questions invite scrutiny; a speaker’s confidence is not a reason to accept every assumption.

Reading invitation: compare chapter 1 on useful possessions with chapters 8–9 on order, then look at chapter 21 on leadership. Could a person have excellent equipment yet manage badly? The English edition linked below calls the work The Economist. Its subject is the oikos—household, estate, and people—rather than economics in the modern national sense.

That layered voice matters. This is not a diary written by the wife or a complete account from every worker. Our adaptation foregrounds practical knowledge and the labor that makes an orderly household function, while identifying new teaching examples as such.

sections.title: Order can save a search
body: A tool placed where people expect to find it reduces wasted effort. Ischomachus uses comparisons, including the compact organization of a ship, to make order seem both useful and impressive. Different things require suitable places.

Make a small plan for a shared work area. Choose three objects and explain why each belongs in its place. Then ask whether another person could understand your arrangement without reading your mind. Order that only its designer understands is fragile.

sections.title: Who makes order possible?
body: The household includes people of unequal status and power, including enslaved laborers. Organization does not erase that inequality. A neat room can conceal whose work keeps it neat and who has authority to change the arrangement.

The lesson asks you to notice expertise: someone must know where an object belongs, be able to move it, and have time to return it. Those are distinct conditions. Do not assume that ownership and practical knowledge belong to the same person.

sections.title: Three verbs, three questions
body: Use κεῖται to ask where an item lies, δύναται to ask who can retrieve it, and ἐπίσταται to ask who knows how to handle it. Explain a case where a person knows how but lacks the opportunity or permission.

The Culture/History banner imagines the organized ship used as a comparison in the dialogue; the Reading banner imagines household work. Neither is an archaeological plan. Look for equipment that can be found and used quickly, then ask who maintains that order. Close with one change that would make your imaginary work area easier for everyone who uses it, and state who should help decide.
